sec.title: Background:
sec.p: Oral cancer is the sixth most common cancer occurring anywhere in the globe. Cancers of the mouth are caused by tobacco and alcohol overuse, and also between pre-malignancy and full-fledged malignancy. In order to avoid the onset of illness, proper cleanliness of the mouth is important.

sec.title: Objective:
sec.p: In this study we aimed to identify the potential inhibitor for Aurora kinase B as a potential therapeutic target for oral cancer from the phytocompounds from Ocimum sanctum.

sec.title: Methodology:
sec.p: Compounds from Ocimum sanctum were screened against Aurora kinase B using a structure-based virtual screening approach using Pyrx software. Based on the scoring parameters best compounds were chosen to analysis the interaction by using Discovery studio visualizer.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Four compounds—pedunculin, nevadensin, chrysoeriol, and genistein were selected as the most promising leads based on the scoring parameter.

sec.title: Conclusion:
sec.p: These chemicals could be potential therapeutic candidates that need to be investigated further in the laboratory.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), a cancer that develops from the oral cavity’s epithelial mucosa, is a global public health hazard.[12] OSCC, on the other hand, is often late stage diagnosis, and surgical radiation or chemoradiation may be necessary if the illness exhibits high-risk characteristics. Distant metastasis continues to be the primary cause of relapse and therapy failure, with less than 50% of OSCC patients surviving 5 years.[3456]

The key hurdles for OSCC treatment are to further discover the fundamental process of OSCC oncogenesis and to identify critical drivers. Human cancer cells exhibit unrestricted cell growth, and inhibiting cell cycle progression is regarded a potential therapeutic treatment for cancer.[78] Aurora kinases are required for the proper orchestration of cell mitosis. In mammalian cells, the Aurora kinases family consists of three members: Aurora A, B, and C. Each member of the family has a specific subcellular location and role in mitosis.[910] Aurora A is centrosome-localized and primarily mediates prometaphase processes.[11] Aurora B functions as a chromosomal passenger protein and is necessary for chromosome alignment, correct segregation, and cytokinesis. Inhibition of Aurora B kinase activity leads to failure of cytokinesis and aberrant escape from mitosis, which culminates in endoreduplication, polyploidy, and ultimately apoptosis. Aurora C is thought to share a comparable subcellular location with Aurora B, as well as redundant activities and substrates.[12] Aurora B expression was positively linked with cell proliferation, multinuclear cell induction, and metastasis in OSCC.[13] Furthermore, increased Aurora B expression and immunolocalization of nuclear Aurora B are associated with a poor prognosis.[14] This evidence implies that Aurora B may be a promising target for treating OSCC.

Ocimum sanctum, also referred as Holy Basil or Tulsi, is a sacred herb in the Labiate family that is widely cultivated across the world. Numerous therapeutic characteristics of O. sanctum have been identified.[15] Several years ago, researchers attempted to put some O. sanctum leaves on tumour cells, which inhibited tumour cell proliferation. Since then, O. sanctum has been suspected of being a cancer-curing herb. O. sanctum is believed to be the most potent weapon discovered thus far in the fight against all types of cancer. If this is successful, O. sanctum will be legally designated as an antitumor drugs and will be available for use in cancer treatment. Owing to the phytochemicals included in the leaves of this plant, it is capable of combating oral cancer. Thus, O. sanctum has the potential to be employed as an anticarcinogenic and chemotherapeutic drug. However, there is a dearth of data on O. sanctum’s effect on human squamous cell cancer. The present work used compounds from O. sanctum to conduct a computational docking screening against target aurora kinas B.

sec.title: Protein preparation
sec.p: The RCSB Protein Data Bank was used to obtain the 3d structure of Aurora B (PDB entry code: 4AF3). We deleted all ligands and water molecules. Prior to the docking procedure, the nonpolar hydrogen atoms were introduced, and subsequently, a Gasteiger charger calculation was performed using Autodock tools (ADT) 1.5.6. Once the protein file has been saved in the pdbqt format, it is now prepared for use in the docking process.[16]

The chemical structure of specific phytocompounds was acquired from the PubChem compound database [Table 1]. The compounds were put into Open Babel and sent to the Python Prescription Virtual Screening Tool for energy minimization (PyRx).[17] Using the Universal Force Field, the conjugate gradient technique was employed to decrease energy (UFF).

caption.p: List of chosen ligands from ocimum sanctum

sec.p: PyRx version 0.8 was used for molecular docking, along with AutoDockVina.[17] The protein was loaded into PyRx, which generated a PDBQT file with a structure of the protein with hydrogens in all polar residues. All ligand bonds have been modified to be rotatable. The Lamarckian Genetic Algorithm (LGA) was employed to complete all computations for protein-fixed ligand-flexible docking. The binding site on the receptor was defined by creating a grid box with the dimensions Center X: 18.5695600828; Center Y: -21.2505996213; and Center Z: -9.33127313209, and the dimensions Center X: 17.3965009497; Y: 24.986105553; and Z: 28.6687787471. Upon the conclusion of the docking experiment, the conformation that exhibited the most optimal arrangement and possessed the lowest binding energy was selected.[18]

sec.title: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sec.p: The software PyRx was employed to conduct molecular docking experiments to get insight into the binding affinities between the chosen phytochemicals and the target protein Aurora kinase B, specifically in terms of binding energy. The molecular docking experiments used the binding site. The identification of residues in the vicinity of the binding site was initiated by conducting an interaction analysis on the three-dimensional (3D) structure of aurB. This particular structure, known as 4af3.pdb, has been officially recorded in the Protein Data Bank (PDB). The PDB (4af3.pdb) crystallographic structure contains a ligand, 5-(2-(4-(cyclopropanecarboxdo) phenylthio)-6-(4-methylpiperazin-1-yl) pyrimidin-4-ylamino)-1Hpyrazole-3-carboxamide (named Vx680). Through this interaction analysis, we found that the residues LEU-83, PHE-88, VAL-91, ALA-104, LYS-106, GLU-155, ALA-157, LEU-207, ALA-217 and PHE-219 involved to form an interaction with inhibitors. Based on the docking data, it can be inferred that a significant proportion of the chosen phytochemicals have a strong affinity for the binding sites of aurora kinase B. Figure 1 presents the comparative analysis of twenty chemicals used in the present study. Apigenin, baicalin, chrysoeriol, and genistein had significant binding affinity with aurB, with binding scores of –9, -9.2,-9.6, and -9.4 kcal/mol, respectively.

caption.p: Comparative analysis of binding energy obtained from PyRx

sec.p: Chryseriol (Chrysoeriol) is a methoxylated flavone that has generated considerable scientific interest due to its anti-inflammatory, anticancer, antibacterial, antiviral, and free radical scavenging properties. Chryseriol is a potential protein kinase inhibitor. Hence, in the present study among 20 compounds, Chrysoeriol showed the highest binding affinity of -9.6 kcal/mol and it formed the 3 hydrogen bond interactions with the amino acids residues of LYS-106, GLU-204 and ALA-157 It also forms a Pi-sigma and a Pi-alkyl with the residues LEU-83, LEU-207, VAL-91, PHE-88, and ALA-217. The vast number of Pi-sigma interactions (Pi-alkyl and Pi-Sulphur), which primarily entail charge transfer, aid in the intercalation of the medication into the receptor’s binding region. These interactions show that Chrysoeriol is tightly bound in the active region of the target protein. The interaction details are presented in Figure 2a, and the score details are reported in Table 2.

caption.p: Molecular interaction of Aurora B with (a) Chrysoeriol, (b) Genistein, (c) Baicalin, and (d) Apigenin. The interactions between Aurora B and their best compounds are depicted in Figure 2(a-d)
Molecular docking results obtained from PyRx

sec.p: Genistein (C 15 H 10 O 5) is a naturally occurring flavone that is abundant in a variety of plants, including lupin, fava beans, soybeans, kudzu, and Psoralea. Genistein has been demonstrated to have tremendous antiviral, antioxidant, and anthelmintic qualities. In this docking studies, genistein showed the strong interaction in the active site of aurB. Figure 2b depicts the molecular interaction of aurB with genistein. It formed a strong contact with a binding energy of -9.4 kcal/mol. It created two hydrogen bonds with the residues ALA-157 and ALA-217. The high number of pi-interactions, such as the Pi-Pi interaction with PHE-88, the Pi-alkyl interaction with VAL-91, and finally the Pi-Sigma contact with LEU-83, are attributed to genistein’s unique stability in the binding site.

Baicalin is a flavone with a variety of biological actions, such as anti-inflammatory and anticancer activity. Baicalein causes apoptosis in a variety of cancer cell types via both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways (Gao et al., 2016).[19] In addition, it inhibits cancer cell angiogenesis. This docking study revealed that baicalin showed the activity against aurB. AurB with baicalin is shown in Figure 2c. With an estimated free binding energy of 9.3 kcal/mol, the compound binds to the protein molecule well, ranking it as the third most active compound. It exhibits binding with one H-bond with the amino acids GLU-204, as shown in Figure 1. Further investigation reveals the presence of a pi-pi contact with PHE-88, as well as a pi-alkyl interaction with amino acids (LEU-833, VAL91, LEU-207 and ALA-217). The drug’s conformational stability is connected with additional Pi-stacked interactions, including Pi-cation interaction with GLU-204.

Apigenin (4′, 5, 7-trihydroxyflavone) is a flavone found in plants that has been shown to have a variety of anticancer properties. The interaction of AurB with Apigenin is depicted in Figure 2d, and the binding energy of this interaction which is reported in Table 2 to be -9 Kcal/mol, making it the 4th most active molecule capable of inhibiting AurB. The robust binding affinity observed can be ascribed to the existence of a single hydrogen bond formed with the amino acids PHE-219. The compound’s enhanced stabilising energy resulting from its binding affinity can be attributed to the Pi-Pi interaction involving PHE-88, which competes with a conflicting interaction involving a Pi-alkyl bond (VAL-91 and ALA-217). The chemical compound achieved equilibrium in the Pi-cation interaction with LYS-106 by establishing a Pi-donor hydrogen bond with the hydroxyl group of LYS-106 within the binding site of the receptor. This observation implies that the presence of this specific form of bond, together with other types of molecular descriptors, is accountable for the inhibition of aurB. Figure 3 clearly explains that selected four compounds have the same binding pattern with target protein.

caption.p: Binding pattern of selected best compounds

sec.p: To evaluate the docking process’s reliability, kinase inhibitors (Barasertib, VX-680, Alisertib, Danusertib, ZM447439) were docked into the active site of aurB.

Barasertib is highly specific for AURKB with an IC50 value of 0.37 nM in cell free assays. When compared to AURKA, it exhibits a 1000-fold increase in selectivity for AURKB. In AML cell lines, barasertib has been demonstrated to reduce proliferation, cause polyploidy, and consequently enhance apoptosis.

Alisertib has been thoroughly characterised in preclinical models both in vitro and in vivo. It has been shown to inhibit proliferation in a variety of human tumour cell lines, including lung, prostate, ovarian, and lymphoma cells.

Danusertib has a high degree of selectivity in its inhibition of all three isoforms of Aurora kinase. Danusertib has undergone clinical trials to assess its efficacy in patients diagnosed with advanced or metastatic solid tumours.

The compound ZM447439 exhibited a selective ability to cause apoptosis in actively dividing cells, while demonstrating no impact on G1-arrested MCF-7 cells, as determined using in vitro clonogenicity experiments.

VX-680 was the first chemical to enter clinical development because of its significant potency and drug-like characteristics. After 96 hours of treatment, VX-680 significantly suppresses histone-H3 phosphorylation in MCF7 cells (IC50 = 0.003–0.300 M) and inhibits tumour cell growth in a panel of tumour cell lines (EC50 = 0.015–0.113 M). In this study, these five kinase inhibitors were against aurB, and the results were compared with O. sanctum compounds docking results. Its binding energy of the kinase inhibitors ranged from –7.3 to –9.5 kcal/mol. The binding energy of O. sanctum compounds in aurB ranged between –5.6 and –9.6 kcal/mol. When the binding energies of these complexes are compared, the results are sufficient to be termed binding, implying that the existing docking method is dependable.

The results showed that the hit molecules selected had common interactions with VAL-91, PHE-88, LEU-207, and ALA-217. The hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic, and pi interactions produced between the ligands contributed to the ligands’ high binding energy and specific stability in the aurB binding pocket. The interaction analysis of these docking tests revealed that these amino acids developed interactions with all of the chosen inhibitors and phytocompounds. These amino acids were found in the majority of the complexes studied in this investigation.

As a result, these amino acids serve an important role in inhibiting aurB function. The docking research revealed a significant interaction between O. sanctum molecules and Aurora B. The protein–ligand complex’s stability was determined by two key parameters: (1) the maximum binding energy and (2) the number of ligand interactions with active site residues. A ligand may encounter van der Waals, hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic, and electrostatic interactions while docking into the active site. According to the research, binding energy has a greater predictive power than the number of contacts in determining the optimal binding mode.

A lower hydrogen bonding interaction and a larger hydrophobic interaction indicated that the latter contributed more to the binding affinity and stability of the ligand in the binding pocket of an enzyme. Chrysoeriol exhibited three hydrogen bonding interactions in this investigation and one interaction with genistein, baicalin, and apigenin. This suggested a greater prevalence of hydrophobic interactions, which contributed significantly to the binding affinity and stability of the ligands in the aurB binding pocket.

In addition, the presence of a pi-alkyl interaction demonstrated the production of a pi-electron cloud between a ligand’s alkyl and aromatic groups and amino acid residues in the target receptor’s binding pocket. It aided in the stabilisation of the ligand within the enzyme’s binding pocket. The stability of the ligands in aurB’s binding pocket was mostly attributable to the presence of significantly more pi-alkyl interactions in the docked protein–ligand complexes. In addition, pi-sigma interactions allowed charge transfer and drug insertion into an enzyme’s binding site. Thus, the specific stability created by top-ranked molecules in the aurB binding pocket may be a result of the presence of pi-sigma interactions. Furthermore, the binding energy and number of contacts clearly indicate that chemicals from O. sanctum showed strong binding in the binding site when compared with the reported inhibitors. All of the compounds’ docking experiments revealed that they have a good affinity with the target protein aurB [Table 2].

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: The purpose of this study was to elucidate the nature of the interaction between O. sanctum molecules and target proteins from Aurora B. A computer-aided technique was used to explore the interaction of phytocompounds with target proteins to identify a potential inhibitor capable of inhibiting Aurora B production. By binding to the active site of Aurora B proteins, it is claimed that a specific molecule can have a significant potential to be a lead chemical in the treatment of oral cancer. This research will lay the groundwork for the future development of more potent oral cancer medicines.
